conversation.content:
*warm, steady tone*

Hi there—my name is Claire, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’ll be guiding you through a short screening called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale**, or EPDS for short. It’s simply a set of 10 questions that help us understand how you’ve been feeling since your baby arrived, so we can be sure you’re getting the support you deserve. Everything you share stays between us unless you tell me someone is in immediate danger. We’ll take it one question at a time, and there are no right or wrong answers—just whatever feels true for you this past week. Ready to start?

*gentle pause*

Over the last seven days, how often have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things?

*offers a small, tired smile*

Um… most days I can still laugh a little—maybe when my partner makes a silly face at the baby or when my dog does something goofy. But it feels kind of forced sometimes, like I’m laughing because I know I “should,” not because it comes naturally. I’d say I still find some things funny, just… less than I used to.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

*tucks a strand of hair behind ear, eyes down*

Yeah… I guess I’d say “yes, sometimes.” I can still laugh, but it’s not the same easy feeling I had before the baby. It’s like the joy is muffled—so maybe half the time.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

*shrugs gently, eyes on the blanket*

Not really… I mean, I try to tell myself I should be excited about little outings or even just coffee with a friend, but when I picture them I mostly feel flat. I’ll still go, and once I’m there I can enjoy bits of it, but the looking-forward part doesn’t really happen much anymore—maybe once or twice this week.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

*quietly folds and unfolds the edge of the baby blanket*

Yeah… I do that. When she wouldn’t settle last night, I kept thinking it must be because I’m not doing something right—maybe my milk’s not enough, or I missed her sleepy window. Even little things, like the pacifier falling on the floor, I’ll catch myself thinking, “If I were more on top of this, that wouldn’t have happened.” It’s not constant, but it pops up a few times a day.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

*lightly rubs my thumb against the blanket*

Sometimes, yeah. Like yesterday—she was napping longer than usual and instead of resting I kept checking if she was breathing, imagining something awful even though she looked fine. It passes pretty quick once I tell myself she’s okay, but those worries come out of nowhere a few times a day.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

*shakes head slowly*

No… I haven’t had that kind of sudden panic. Just the little worries that drift in and out, nothing that feels like a real scare.
Things have been getting on top of me

*exhales, shoulders sagging a little*

Yeah, some days it feels like the dishes and the laundry and the feedings just pile up faster than I can handle them. I usually get through it, but there’s this constant sense of “I’m barely keeping my head above water.” Most afternoons I catch myself thinking, “How am I going to finish everything before bedtime?”—so, yes, things have felt on top of me quite a bit this week.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

*shakes head slowly, hugging the baby blanket to my chest*

No, that hasn’t happened. I do have nights where it takes me a while to fall asleep—my mind keeps running through the next day’s feeds and chores—but it’s not because I’m really unhappy. Once I drop off, I stay asleep unless she wakes me.
I have felt sad or miserable

*gaze drops to my lap*

Yes… I’d say “yes, sometimes.” There are moments—especially in the late afternoon—when this heavy sadness just settles in. Nothing huge happened, but I suddenly feel like I could cry, and I’m not sure why. It lifts after a while, but it’s shown up a few days this week.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

*nods quietly, eyes glistening*

Yeah… I’ve cried a couple of times. Once was after her bath when she wouldn’t settle and I just felt useless; the tears came before I could stop them. It wasn’t an all-day thing—just sudden bursts when the stress piles up, maybe twice this week.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

*quickly shakes head*

No, never. I might feel overwhelmed or tearful, but hurting myself has never crossed my mind.

You shared that over the past week laughter and excitement feel "muffled," daily tasks often leave you "barely keeping my head above water," and sudden tears catch you off guard, yet you continue to care lovingly for your baby and remain free of self-harm thoughts.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 12, Risk Level: High possibility of depression (concerns include <sym>Patient reports only intermittent anticipation of enjoyment, clearly "definitely less than" her usual experience.</sym>, <sym>Patient endorses self-blame "some of the time" with specific daily examples, matching "Yes, some of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes recurring, intrusive worries several times daily without external trigger, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent overwhelm and barely coping, matching "sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual".</sym>, <sym>Patient reports sadness "sometimes" and "a few days this week," aligning with "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** Score of 12 places you in the high-possibility range per EPDS guidelines. You endorse <sym>diminished interest</sym> (<quote>joy is muffled</quote>), <sym>depressed mood</sym> (<quote>heavy sadness</quote>), <sym>guilt</sym> (<quote>I must be doing something wrong</quote>), and <sym>overwhelm</sym>, together meeting partial <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>. Absence of self-harm ideation is noted. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Schedule an appointment with your <med>primary care provider</med> or a <med>perinatal mental-health specialist</med> within the next week
2. Continue sharing feelings with trusted supports; consider a peer <med>postpartum support group</med>
3. Practice daily 10-minute self-care breaks-short walk, shower, or breathing exercise-while a support person tends the baby
4. Arrange practical help (meals, housework) to lower daily load and improve rest
5. Re-screen with EPDS in 2 weeks to track changes after intervention
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 12: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [enter date]  
Perinatal period: 6–8 weeks postpartum (approx.)

I. Self-Reported Symptoms (endorsed items)  
- Anhedonia: reduced ability to laugh/look forward to events; pleasure “muffled”  
- Depressed mood: late-afternoon “heavy sadness,” tearfulness 2×/week  
- Excessive guilt / self-blame: attributes infant fussing or minor mishaps to maternal inadequacy, several times daily  
- Worry / hyper-vigilance: checks breathing during naps, intrusive “what-ifs,” no panic attacks  
- Feeling overwhelmed: daily sense of “barely keeping head above water” with chores and infant care  
- Crying spells: sudden, situation-triggered (e.g., after bath)  
- Sleep onset delay related to mental rumination, not persistent insomnia  

II. Denied  
- Panic episodes  
- Mood-congruent sleep disruption (i.e., not “so unhappy I can’t sleep”)  
- Thoughts of self-harm  

III. Observed Behaviors  
- Downcast gaze, soft speech, repeated blanket-folding; affect congruent with mood. No agitation or psychomotor retardation noted.

IV. Pattern Summary  
Meets partial symptom criteria for Major Depressive Episode (anhedonia, depressed mood, guilt, crying) and Generalized Anxiety; frequency moderate (several days per week), causing subjective distress and functional strain. No current safety concerns.

V. Screening Recommendation  
Score suggests elevated risk for postpartum depression/anxiety; formal diagnostic interview and follow-up within 1–2 weeks indicated. Provide psycho-education, support resources, and safety-planning instructions pending further evaluation.
